reasoning: The gold answer treats 'not asleep' and 'awake' as the same proposition (merged to one symbol), but the skill's guidance explicitly instructs the opposite for a similar-looking pair ('not raining'/'dry'), and gives no way to distinguish direct lexical antonyms (asleep/awake) from merely correlated states (raining/dry). Add a rule clarifying that direct antonym pairs where one word IS the negation-equivalent of the other should merge, while correlated-but-distinct states should not.

edits.target: - Reuse the same symbol only when two phrasings are near-certainly the same claim (e.g. "not raining" and "dry" are NOT the same claim — keep them separate; "the lights are off" and "the room is not lit" ARE the same claim — merge them).
edits.content: - Reuse the same symbol only when two phrasings are near-certainly the same claim (e.g. "not raining" and "dry" are NOT the same claim — keep them separate, since dryness and rain are merely correlated, not logical negations of each other; "the lights are off" and "the room is not lit" ARE the same claim — merge them). Direct lexical antonym pairs where one state is definitionally the absence/opposite of the other (e.g. "asleep"/"awake", "alive"/"dead", "open"/"closed") count as the SAME proposition under negation: "not asleep" and "awake" both map to `¬P` where P="asleep" (or equivalently both map to the same symbol), not to two separate symbols.
